Report a benchmark with intervals

Source: R/core-bench-report.R
hr_report.Rd

Turns the scored rows of an hr_benchmark() into accuracy with intervals that respect clustering, paired differences between arms, stability across runs, pass^k, cost, the cost-accuracy frontier, failure counts and variance components. Only rows with reportable = TRUE are used, so the dev split never enters a report, and items with no label are left out.

Usage

hr_report(
  bench,
  contrasts = NULL,
  B = 2000,
  conf = 0.95,
  k = c(1, 3, 5),
  seed = 1,
  method = c("auto", "bootstrap", "cluster_t", "bayes", "exact"),
  confirmatory = FALSE,
  registration = NULL
)

# S3 method for class 'hr_bench_report'
print(x, digits = 3, ...)

# S3 method for class 'hr_bench_report'
as_json(x, pretty = TRUE, ...)

Arguments

bench

An hr_benchmark() result, or a data frame with at least the columns cluster, item, arm, run and correct. Optional columns (reportable, outcome, failure_kind, usd, usd_provenance, tokens_in, tokens_out) are used when present. Every arm must have every run on every item, and an item is scored on every run or on none.

contrasts

Pairs of arms to compare: a two-column character matrix of arm names, each row giving first minus second. NULL compares every pair, in benchmark order.

B

Number of cluster bootstrap resamples, at least 100.

conf

Confidence level of every interval.

k

The values of k for pass^k.

seed

Seed of the private random stream the resamples are drawn from; the caller's random state is left as it was.

method

"auto", "bootstrap", "cluster_t", "bayes" or "exact", as above.

confirmatory

TRUE for a confirmatory report, which raises the default B to 5000 and refuses dev-split rows. Left unset, it is TRUE when registration holds a confirmatory contrast.

registration

An hr_register_contrasts() result for the reference this benchmark scored, or NULL.

x

An hr_bench_report.

digits

Digits to print.

...

Ignored by print(); passed on by as_json().

pretty

Whether to indent the JSON.

Value

An object of class hr_bench_report, a list with

method, method_reason, descriptive

The interval method used for accuracy, why it was chosen, and whether the report is descriptive only.

n_items, n_clusters, runs, arms, conf, B, seed, confirmatory

The design and settings.

accuracy

Per arm: estimate, lower, upper, method ("studentised_cluster_bootstrap", "logit_cluster_robust_t", "korn_graubard_clopper_pearson", "beta_binomial_bayes" or "descriptive"), and the rank interval rank_lower, rank_upper.

bayes

Per arm, in the Bayesian regime: posterior mean and median of mu and posterior mean of rho.

contrasts

Per contrast: arm1, arm2, estimate (arm1 minus arm2), lower, upper, method ("cluster_robust_t", or "tango_items" when the cluster variance is 0).

simultaneous

Every pairwise difference with simultaneous lower and upper bounds, method ("max_t_cluster_robust", or "tango_items" when the cluster variance is 0) and the max-t critical value (NA on "tango_items" rows, which do not use it).

stability

Per arm: flip_rate, tara, run_sd.

pass_k

Per arm and k: pass_k with lower and upper.

cost

Per arm: usd_per_item, usd_per_correct, tokens_per_item, tokens_per_correct, each with _lower and _upper, usd_estimated_share and estimated_flag.

frontier

Per arm: usd_per_item, accuracy, on_frontier, frontier_share.

failures

Per arm: counts by failure kind, accuracy and accuracy_without_parse_refusal.

variance

within, between, within_share overall and per arm, and recommend_runs.

ni

With a registration, per registered contrast: new, reference, label, margin, estimate, the one-sided lower bound at the one-sided level it was tested at, accuracy_holds, cost_test, cost_diff, cost_upper, cost_holds, verdict, mdd_design, mdd_achieved, and Tango's tango_lower and tango_upper with tango_agrees (whether it reaches the same accuracy conclusion), the effective number of pairs n_eff it rests on, and p_value, the smallest one-sided level at which the contrast passes, found by bisection. The search stops at 1e-6, and for a contrast with cost_test = TRUE at 1 / (B + 1), the smallest level the B bootstrap resamples of the cost bound resolve (1 / 2001, about 5.0e-4, at B = 2000); a value at that floor means at most the floor. NULL without one.

registration

The registration's hash, time and reference hash, or NULL.

notes

What the reader should know.

Details

Accuracy. For each arm, the mean correctness over runs within each item, then the mean over items.

Intervals. With method = "auto" the method follows the size of the benchmark. Both rest on the cluster sums of item accuracy: accuracy is the ratio estimator r = sum_c S_c / sum_c n_c, with S_c the summed item accuracy and n_c the items of cluster c, and its cluster-robust (linearised) variance is V = C / (C - 1) * sum_c (S_c - r n_c)^2 / N^2, with the small-sample factor C / (C - 1) for C clusters and N items (Cochran 1977, chapter 6; Cameron and Miller 2015).

  • At least 300 items and at least 30 clusters (method = "bootstrap"): a studentised (bootstrap-t) cluster bootstrap (Efron and Tibshirani 1993, chapter 12; Davison and Hinkley 1997, chapters 2 and 5). Each of the B resamples draws whole clusters with replacement, with all their items, runs and arms, and gives t* = (r* - r) / se*, with se* the linearised standard error of the resample. The interval is [r - q_hi se, r - q_lo se], with q_lo and q_hi the (1 - conf) / 2 and (1 + conf) / 2 quantiles of t* and se = sqrt(V), cut to [0, 1]. Studentising corrects the skew of a proportion near a bound, where the BCa interval this replaces undercovered (93.5% at a true accuracy of 0.75 in the coverage simulation of dev/sim-coverage.R, 386 items in 40 clusters); the studentised interval covered 95.5% and 95.0% there.

  • Below either threshold (method = "cluster_t"): a cluster-robust t interval on the logit scale, logit(r) plus and minus t_(C - 1, (1 + conf) / 2) x sqrt(V) / (r (1 - r)), mapped back to (0, 1) (the delta method on the logit scale, Agresti 2013; t quantiles with C - 1 degrees of freedom for few clusters, Cameron and Miller 2015). In the coverage simulation (50 items in 10 clusters, 2000 replicates) it covered 95.7% and 95.8%, and 95.2% and 95.8% over 6000 further replicates: slightly conservative, as a t interval is when cluster means are bounded.

  • Where those intervals are not defined, because accuracy is 0 or 1 or every cluster has the same accuracy (V = 0), the arm gets the Korn-Graubard interval below, one-sided from the bound at 0 or 1 at level conf, and its method column and a note say so.

  • method = "exact" selects instead a Clopper-Pearson interval on the effective number of items computed from cluster totals of item accuracy, with Korn and Graubard's (1998) degrees-of-freedom adjustment. Items, not runs, are the trials, since runs of one item mostly agree. It is conservative: 98.4% to 98.8% coverage in the small simulated design.

  • method = "bayes" selects a Bayesian beta-binomial model with a cluster random effect (Bowyer et al. 2025). Cluster c has m_c scored runs over its items, x_c of them correct. Its accuracy is Beta with mean mu and intra-cluster correlation rho, so alpha = mu (1 - rho) / rho and beta = (1 - mu) (1 - rho) / rho, and its runs are binomial given it. The priors on mu and rho are flat (uniform on 0 to 1), the posterior is computed on a grid, and the interval is the equal-tailed credible interval of mu, one-sided from the bound when accuracy is 0 or 1. It is not the default: in the small simulated design it covered 96.5% to 96.6% and its misses fell mostly below the truth (2.9% to 3.2% below, 0.2% to 0.5% above). The prior on rho drives this: the flat prior keeps much of its mass on strong clustering (posterior mean of rho 0.23), which widens the interval and spreads mu toward 0.5. In a check of 600 replicates, a Beta(1, 10) prior on rho balanced the misses but undercovered (91.7% to 92.0%), and a prior uniform on log((1 - rho) / rho) covered 94.5% to 94.8% with misses still lopsided (3.2% to 3.5% below, 2.0% above); counting items instead of runs as trials made it more conservative (98.0% to 98.2% over 2000 replicates), not less lopsided. A prior chosen to hit 95% in one design would not carry to others, so the model is kept as it was, as an option, and a note gives its calibration when it is used. Note that mu is the mean of cluster accuracies, each cluster weighted alike, while the estimate printed beside it weights clusters by their items.

No interval treats items or runs as independent trials (the Wald interval on n items). method = "bootstrap" or "cluster_t" forces that method at any size, with a note when the bootstrap is used below the thresholds, where it is unstable.

Paired differences. For each contrast, accuracy of the first arm minus the second, item by item, so each difference is paired. The mean paired difference is the ratio estimator of the cluster sums of item differences, and its interval is the cluster-robust t interval d plus and minus t_(C - 1, (1 + conf) / 2) x sqrt(V_d), with V_d the linearised variance above applied to the differences, whatever the method for accuracy (Cameron and Miller 2015), cut to [-1, 1] as the accuracy intervals are cut to [0, 1] (with few clusters the t quantile can reach past either end). It covered 94.7% (40 clusters) and 95.7% (10 clusters) in the coverage simulation, where the BCa cluster bootstrap it replaces covered 92.9% and 89.2%. When every cluster gives the same mean difference per item, V_d is 0 and the t interval is not defined. That is a property of the items, not evidence that the difference is known, so the interval then takes the items, not the clusters, as the sampling units: Tango's (1998) score interval for paired proportions with the discordant shares q10 and q01 described under non-inferiority below, on n_eff = I x (z_(1 - a) / t_(C - 1, 1 - a))^2 pairs for one-sided level a = (1 - conf) / 2, the I items scaled for the C - 1 degrees of freedom as Korn and Graubard's effective size is. Its method is "tango_items", and a note says so.

Rankings. No leaderboard by point estimate: arms are listed in the order of the benchmark. Simultaneous intervals over all pairwise differences use the single-step max-t method (Hothorn, Bretz and Westfall 2008) on the same cluster-robust t statistics: the critical value is the conf quantile of the largest absolute value of a multivariate t with C - 1 degrees of freedom and the correlation matrix of the linearised covariance of the differences, from 100000 draws of the private random stream. With one pair it is the t quantile of the paired interval. A pair whose V_d is 0 gets the Tango interval above at the Bonferroni level a = (1 - conf) / (2 x number of pairs), and the max-t critical value over the other pairs is then taken at 1 - (1 - conf) x (pairs with V_d > 0) / (number of pairs), so the error rates of the two parts add up to at most 1 - conf over the whole family. With 3 pairs of which 1 has V_d = 0 and conf = 0.95, the max-t part runs at 1 - 0.05 x 2 / 3, about 0.967. These intervals are cut to [-1, 1] too. Rank intervals are the (1 - conf) / 2 and (1 + conf) / 2 quantiles of each arm's rank over the cluster bootstrap resamples (rank 1 is the most accurate).

Stability (Atil et al. 2025): the flip rate is the share of items whose correctness differs across runs; TARa is the share of items whose scored output (outcome, or the failure kind when there is none) is the same on every run; the run-level SD is the standard deviation over runs of each run's accuracy. Agreement of one arm with itself is stability, not accuracy.

Reliability: pass^k (Yao et al. 2024), the chance that k runs drawn without replacement from an item's runs are all correct, estimated without bias as the mean over items of choose(c_i, k) / choose(R, k), with c_i the item's correct runs out of R. Values of k above the number of runs are left out. An item must be scored on every run or on none, so R is the same for every item.

Cost (Kapoor et al. 2024): dollars and tokens (in plus out) per item, the mean over runs and then items, and per correct item, the total over runs divided by the correct runs. An arm whose dollars rest on estimated token counts for more than 5% of its spend is flagged.

Frontier: the Pareto set on dollars per item and accuracy, and for each arm the share of bootstrap resamples in which it is on the frontier. The share is an extension of Kapoor et al., not a published standard.

Failures: counts by failure kind. Every failure counts as wrong in the accuracy above; a sensitivity line gives accuracy with parse failures and refusals left out instead.

Variance components, on the probability scale. With p_ia the accuracy of item i under arm a over runs, the within-item run variance is the mean of p_ia (1 - p_ia) over item-arm cells, and the between-item variance is the variance of p_ia over items, averaged over arms. When the within share exceeds 10%, runs = 10 is recommended.

Non-inferiority. With a registration from hr_register_contrasts(), each registered contrast is tested. The verdict holds only if (1) the one-sided lower bound of the accuracy difference (new minus reference) is above -margin and (2), when the contrast has cost_test = TRUE, the one-sided upper bound of the paired difference in dollars per item is below 0. The accuracy bound is the cluster-robust t bound of the paired differences above, taken one-sided: d - t_(C - 1, 1 - level) x sqrt(V_d), or, when V_d is 0, the lower end of the Tango interval with items as pairs above at one-sided level. At a one-sided level of 0.025 that is the 97.5% bound, the lower end of the 95% contrast interval, so the verdict and the printed interval agree. The cost bound is the BCa cluster bootstrap of the cost intervals. Each contrast's p-value is the smallest one-sided level at which both conditions hold (an intersection-union test, so each condition runs at that full level). The confirmatory contrasts are tested with Holm's (1979) step-down procedure at the registration's alpha: in order of their p-values, the j-th of k is tested at alpha / (k - j + 1), and the first that fails stops the procedure. Exploratory contrasts are tested at alpha alone. Beside every verdict the report gives the design MDD the contrast was registered against and the achieved MDD, (t_(C - 1, 1 - alpha') + t_(C - 1, power)) x SE, with SE = sqrt(V_d) the linearised standard error of the paired difference (the hr_mdd() formula with p_disc / n_eff taken from the data) and alpha' = alpha / (number of confirmatory contrasts), or alpha for an exploratory one; it is NA when V_d is 0, since the data then give no variance to base it on. A verdict that passed its registered test is shown as passed even when the achieved MDD exceeds the margin; a note says so. As a cross-check, Tango's (1998) score interval for paired proportions is computed on effective counts. The discordant shares are the means over items of the chance that a run of the new arm is right and a run of the reference wrong (q10), and the reverse (q01). The effective number of pairs is (q10 + q01 - estimate^2) / SE^2, the size of a simple paired sample with the linearised variance V_d (the effective size of Korn and Graubard 1998, applied to the paired difference), at most the number of items (runs of one item mostly agree, so they are not independent pairs); the counts are q10 and q01 times it. Tango's interval is reported at the level the contrast was tested at, beside whether it reaches the same accuracy conclusion, and is not used in the verdict.

A registration, or confirmatory = TRUE, makes the report evidence: a bench with any row outside the test and final splits (dev, exploratory or calibration) or marked not reportable is then refused with an error of class hr_dev_not_evidence. The bench must carry the hash of the reference the registration names, as an hr_benchmark() result does (error class hr_registration_mismatch), and a registration changed after it was made is refused (class hr_registration_changed).

Below 5 runs the report is descriptive only: point estimates without intervals, resamples or rank intervals. Cost and pass^k intervals (BCa), rank intervals and the frontier share come from the cluster bootstrap in both regimes; below the thresholds the report says to read them as rough.

References

Atil, B. et al. (2025). Non-determinism of "deterministic" LLM settings. arXiv:2408.04667.

Agresti, A. (2013). Categorical Data Analysis, 3rd edition. Wiley.

Bowyer, S. et al. (2025). Position: Don't use the CLT in LLM evals with fewer than a few hundred datapoints. ICML 2025.

Cameron, A. C. and Miller, D. L. (2015). A practitioner's guide to cluster-robust inference. Journal of Human Resources 50(2), 317-372.

Cochran, W. G. (1977). Sampling Techniques, 3rd edition. Wiley.

Davison, A. C. and Hinkley, D. V. (1997). Bootstrap Methods and their Application. Cambridge University Press.

Efron, B. (1987). Better bootstrap confidence intervals. Journal of the American Statistical Association 82(397), 171-185.

Efron, B. and Tibshirani, R. J. (1993). An Introduction to the Bootstrap. Chapman and Hall.

Hothorn, T., Bretz, F. and Westfall, P. (2008). Simultaneous inference in general parametric models. Biometrical Journal 50(3), 346-363.

Kapoor, S., Stroebl, B., Siegel, Z. S., Nadgir, N. and Narayanan, A. (2024). arXiv:2407.01502.

Korn, E. L. and Graubard, B. I. (1998). Confidence intervals for proportions with small expected number of positive counts estimated from survey data. Survey Methodology 24(2), 193-201.

Holm, S. (1979). A simple sequentially rejective multiple test procedure. Scandinavian Journal of Statistics 6(2), 65-70.

Miller, E. (2024). Adding error bars to evals: a statistical approach to language model evaluations. arXiv:2411.00640.

Tango, T. (1998). Equivalence test and confidence interval for the difference in proportions for the paired-sample design. Statistics in Medicine 17(8), 891-908.

Yao, S., Shinn, N., Razavi, P. and Narasimhan, K. (2024). tau-bench. arXiv:2406.12045.

Examples

# 12 documents with 3 questions each, two arms, 5 runs.
set.seed(2)
grid <- expand.grid(run = 1:5, arm = c("short", "long"), item = 1:36,
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
grid$cluster <- paste0("doc", (grid$item - 1) %/% 3 + 1)
grid$item <- paste0("q", grid$item)
grid$correct <- runif(nrow(grid)) < ifelse(grid$arm == "long", 0.8, 0.7)
grid$usd <- ifelse(grid$arm == "long", 0.004, 0.001)
rpt <- hr_report(grid, B = 500)
rpt

#>  short - long -0.167     [-0.256, -0.077] [-0.256, -0.077]
